unit.unitOverview: Numbers are the one part of a language you cannot afford to be approximately right about. A wrong word in a sentence is usually repaired by the person listening; a wrong number costs money, or a missed appointment, or the wrong size delivered. This unit covers ordinals, asking how much and how many, comparing two things, and saying roughly how much of something there is when you do not have an exact figure. It ends with a receipt, because reading one is how you find out whether you were charged what you expected.
unit.learningPath:

Read the three texts aloud. The third is a receipt, and the exercise on it is the one that matters.
Do the Practice. Practice 4 is the one to do slowly.
Record yourself saying prices and amounts, and play it back.

visual.lectureScript:
In Unit 1 you learned the numbers themselves — thirteen and thirty, forty-four, a hundred. This unit is what you do with them.
Four patterns.
The first is ordinals. A cardinal number counts: one, two, three. An ordinal number puts things in order: first, second, third.
Most of them are simple — you add th. Four, fourth. Six, sixth. Ten, tenth. Twenty, twentieth.
Three are irregular and you have to learn them: one becomes first, two becomes second, three becomes third. Everything built on them follows: twenty-first, thirty-second, forty-third.
And two have a spelling change worth noticing: five becomes fifth, not fiveth. Twelve becomes twelfth.
You already used ordinals in Unit 1 for dates — the fourteenth of March. Here you also need them for floors, for positions in a queue, and for steps in a set of instructions. The third floor. The second on the left. First, do this. Second, do that.
Second pattern: how much and how many. These both ask about quantity, and English chooses between them based on the thing, not on the amount.
How many for things you can count. How many people. How many rooms. How many keys.
How much for things you cannot count separately. How much water. How much time. How much money.
And the one you will use most: how much is it? That is asking a price, and the price is not countable, so it is always how much. Never how many is it.
Third pattern: comparing two things. English adds er to a short adjective and follows it with than. Cheaper than. Bigger than. Heavier than.
Watch the spelling. Big becomes bigger, with two g's. Heavy becomes heavier, with the y turning into i. Those two changes cover most of the words you will need.
For longer adjectives, English does not add er. It puts more in front instead: more expensive, more difficult, more comfortable. The rough rule is that words of one syllable take er, words of three or more take more, and words of two go either way. Do not spend time on the rule — you will pick it up by hearing it.
And there are two irregulars you cannot avoid: good becomes better, and bad becomes worse. Not gooder. Not badder.
Fourth pattern: saying how much when you do not have a number. Some. A lot of. A little. A few.
A lot of works with everything. A lot of money, a lot of people.
But a little and a few split the same way as how much and how many. A few for things you can count: a few people, a few days. A little for things you cannot: a little water, a little time, a little money.
This is the same countable and uncountable division you met in pattern two, and once you see it is the same division, you only have to learn it once.
One last thing, and it is practical. Numbers are the one place where being approximately right is not good enough. If you did not catch a price, ask. Use the phrases from the last unit — sorry, can you repeat that? how much did you say? People repeat numbers without minding, because everybody mishears numbers, in every language.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: The One Thing You Cannot Be Nearly Right About
readings.passageScript:
In most of a conversation, being nearly right is enough. If you say she like it instead of she likes it, nothing is lost. The listener repairs it without noticing.
Numbers are different.
If you hear fifteen and the price was fifty, nobody repairs anything. You hand over the wrong money, or you agree to something you did not mean, or you arrive on the wrong day.
So treat numbers as a separate skill, and give yourself permission to stop the conversation for them.
Three habits worth building.
First, repeat the number back. Fifty? Not as a challenge — as a check. The other person will say yes, or they will say no, five-zero, and either way you now know.
Second, ask for it written down when it matters. Can you write it down? is a normal request when money or a date is involved. Nobody is offended.
Third, learn the pairs that sound alike, and check them every time: thirteen and thirty, fourteen and forty, fifteen and fifty, sixteen and sixty.
The difference between them is small in fast speech, and native speakers mishear these too. When they do, they ask. Do the same.

readings.title: How Prices Are Written and Said
readings.passageScript:
A price on a label is not always the price you pay, and the words around it change what it means.
Each means the price is for one item. Four each means four for one of them, not four for all of them.
Per kilo means the price is for one kilo. If the bag weighs half a kilo, you pay half. If it weighs two kilos, you pay double. This is the one that surprises people most, because the number on the shelf is not the number at the till.
From means the cheapest one costs this, and most of them cost more. Rooms from 40 means one room costs 40 and the rest cost more than that.
Up to means the opposite — this is the maximum, and most are less.
Offers are written short and are worth reading slowly. Three for two means you take three and pay for two. Buy one get one free means the same thing with two. Half price means what it says.
And two words that look similar and are not:
Including means it is already in the price.
Excluding means it is not, and will be added.
So delivery included and delivery excluded are opposite statements, and they are often printed in the same small type at the bottom.
When you are not sure, ask: is that the final price? It is a short question and it prevents most surprises.

grammar.title: First, second, third: putting things in order
grammar.explanation: A counting number says how many. An ordinal says which position. You have already used these for dates in Unit 1 — here you need them for floors, queues and steps in instructions.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
four → fourth      ten → tenth
six  → sixth       twenty → twentieth

Three irregulars, learn them:
one → first
two → second
three → third

Two spelling changes:
five → fifth  (not fiveth)
twelve → twelfth

Built on the irregulars: twenty-first, thirty-second, forty-third.
grammar.workedExample:
Write the ordinal for 21.
1. Split it: 20 and 1.
2. The last part decides the ending. The last part is 1.
3. One is irregular: one becomes first.
4. Join: twenty-first.
Result: twenty-first.
The same works for 32 — the last part is 2, so it is thirty-second. Only the LAST part changes; twenty stays twenty.
grammar.commonMistake: Writing fiveth and twelveth. These two change their spelling before the ending, and no rule predicts it — they simply have to be learned. The other common slip is changing the wrong part of a compound: twentieth-first instead of twenty-first.
grammar.memoryTip: Only the last part of the number becomes an ordinal.
grammar.practice:
Write the ordinal.
1. 2
2. 5
3. 9
4. 12
5. 21
6. 33
Then use one in a sentence about a floor.
grammar.answerKey:
1. second  2. fifth  3. ninth  4. twelfth  5. twenty-first  6. thirty-third
Number 3 is worth noting: nine loses its e — ninth, not nineth. So there are three spelling changes to watch, not two: fifth, ninth, twelfth.
A floor sentence should look like: The office is on the third floor.

grammar.title: How much and how many
grammar.explanation: Both ask about quantity. English chooses between them based on whether the thing can be counted separately, not on how large the amount is.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
how many + things you can count
  how many people · how many rooms · how many days

how much + things you cannot count
  how much water · how much time · how much money

Asking a price is always:
  How much is it?  How much does it cost?
  NEVER how many is it.
grammar.workedExample:
Which one: ____ time have we got?
1. Ask: can I count time? Can I say one time, two times, three times, meaning amounts of time? No — that means occasions, not duration.
2. Time as an amount cannot be counted separately.
3. Uncountable takes how much.
Result: How much time have we got?
Now compare: How many days have we got? Days CAN be counted, so it takes many. Same idea, different word, because one is countable and one is not.
grammar.commonMistake: How many is it? when asking a price. Money is uncountable in English even though coins are countable, so the price question is always how much. This is worth fixing because you will ask it several times a day.
grammar.memoryTip: Can you put a number in front of it? Then it is many.
grammar.practice:
Write how much or how many.
1. ____ does it cost?
2. ____ people are waiting?
3. ____ water do you need?
4. ____ rooms has it got?
5. ____ time have we got?
6. ____ kilos do you want?
grammar.answerKey:
1. How much  2. How many  3. How much  4. How many  5. How much  6. How many
Number 6 is the interesting one. Water is uncountable, but kilos are countable — so once you measure something uncountable, the unit becomes countable and takes many. How much water, but how many kilos.

small → smaller than

Spelling changes:
big → bigger  (double the last letter)
heavy → heavier  (y becomes i)

Long adjectives take more:
expensive → more expensive than
difficult → more difficult than

Two irregulars:
good → better      bad → worse
grammar.workedExample:
Compare: this bag (2 kg) and that bag (5 kg).
1. Choose the adjective: heavy.
2. Is it short? Two syllables ending in y — it takes er.
3. Apply the spelling change: y becomes i, so heavier.
4. Add than and the second thing: heavier than this one.
Result: That bag is heavier than this one.
The test for than: if you can ask heavier than WHAT, and there is no answer in the sentence, the sentence is not finished.
grammar.commonMistake: Two things. Leaving out than — this one is cheaper, when you meant cheaper than that one. And doubling up: more cheaper, which uses both methods at once. Use er OR more, never both.
grammar.memoryTip: A comparison needs two things. If only one is named, it is incomplete.
grammar.practice:

2. The market is ____ (cheap) than the shop.
3. This room is ____ (big) than the other one.
4. The train is ____ (expensive) than the bus.
5. This one is ____ (good) than that one.
6. The weather is ____ (bad) today than yesterday.
grammar.answerKey:
1. heavier  2. cheaper  3. bigger  4. more expensive  5. better  6. worse
Check three things. Number 1 changed y to i. Number 3 doubled the g. Numbers 5 and 6 are the irregulars — not gooder, not badder, and they never take more either.

grammar.title: Some, a lot of, a little, a few
grammar.explanation: These say roughly how much without giving a number. Two of them split on exactly the same line as how much and how many — so if you have that division, you already have this one.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
a lot of  → works with everything
  a lot of money · a lot of people

a few     → things you can count
  a few people · a few days · a few questions

a little  → things you cannot count
  a little water · a little time · a little money

some      → works with everything
  some rice · some questions
grammar.workedExample:
Which one: I have ____ time before the bus.
1. Ask: can I count time as an amount? No.
2. Uncountable takes a little.
Result: I have a little time before the bus.
Now change the noun to minutes: I have a few minutes before the bus. Minutes can be counted, so it takes a few. The amount of time is the same — only whether it is countable has changed.
grammar.commonMistake: A few water and a little people are the two errors, and they come from choosing by size rather than by countability. The amount does not decide it. Ask only whether you could put a number in front.
grammar.memoryTip: Same division as how much and how many. Learn it once, use it twice.
grammar.practice:

6. I have ____ questions.
grammar.answerKey:
1. a little  2. a few  3. a little  4. a few  5. a little  6. a few
The rule works every time: could you put a number in front of the noun? Two people, four days, six questions — yes, so a few. Two moneys, four rices, six waters — no, so a little.

activities.title: Practice 4 — A few or a little
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Part A. Sort these into COUNTABLE and UNCOUNTABLE.
days · water · people · money · questions · time · coins · rice · minutes · sugar
Part B. Now write a few or a little.
1. I have ____ money left.
2. There are ____ people outside.
3. Give me ____ sugar, please.

5. I need ____ time.
6. I have ____ questions.

Part A. COUNTABLE: days, people, questions, coins, minutes. UNCOUNTABLE: water, money, time, rice, sugar.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Read the receipt
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Use the receipt in Reading 3. Find each answer directly.
1. How many different items were bought?
2. What was the price of one bar of soap?
3. What was the rice priced at per kilo?
4. What was the subtotal?
5. How much did the offer take off?
6. What was the total?
7. How much change was given?
8. How long do you have to return something?

activities.title: Practice 6 — Check a real number
activities.instructionsAndItems:
This week, do this three times.
When someone tells you a number out loud — a price, a time, a platform, a room — repeat it back to them as a question before you act on it.
Write down what happened each time: what you heard, what they said, and whether you had it right.
activities.answerSummary:
There is no key — the point is what happens, not what is correct.
What most people find: you were right most times, and the once you were wrong would have cost you something. That single catch is the whole reason for the habit.
What also happens: nobody minds. Nobody has ever minded. If you were expecting the other person to be irritated and they were not, write that down too, because that expectation is what usually stops learners from checking.

1. How much  2. How many  3. How much  4. How many  5. How much  6. How many
Number 6 is the interesting one. Water is uncountable, but kilos are countable — so once you measure something uncountable, the unit becomes countable and takes many. How much water, but how many kilos.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. heavier  2. cheaper  3. bigger  4. more expensive  5. better  6. worse
Check three things. Number 1 changed y to i. Number 3 doubled the g. Numbers 5 and 6 are the irregulars — not gooder, not badder, and they never take more either.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. a little  2. a few  3. a little  4. a few  5. a little  6. a few
The rule works every time: could you put a number in front of the noun? Two people, four days, six questions — yes, so a few. Two moneys, four rices, six waters — no, so a little.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. first  2. second  3. third  4. fifth  5. eighth  6. ninth  7. twelfth  8. twentieth  9. twenty-first  10. thirty-second
Four to watch. Five loses its e (fifth). Nine loses its e (ninth). Twelve changes to twelfth. Eight already ends in t, so it takes only h — eighth, with one t, not eightth.
Eight or more correct means this is finished.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. How much  2. How many  3. How much  4. How many  5. How much  6. How many  7. How much  8. How many  9. How much  10. How many  11. How much  12. How many
Every pair here is deliberate: rice and kilos, water and bottles, change and coins. In each pair the substance is uncountable and the container or unit is countable. That is the whole rule — it is the noun you actually wrote that decides, not the thing in the world.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. cheaper  2. bigger  3. heavier  4. lighter  5. wider  6. taller  7. more expensive  8. more difficult  9. better  10. worse
Three kinds here. Short words add er (1, 4, 5, 6). Two change their spelling first — big doubles the g, heavy turns y into i. Wide already ends in e, so it only adds r. Long words take more (7, 8). Two are irregular and follow no rule at all (9, 10).
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
Part A. COUNTABLE: days, people, questions, coins, minutes. UNCOUNTABLE: water, money, time, rice, sugar.
Part B. 1. a little  2. a few  3. a little  4. a few  5. a little  6. a few
Notice money is uncountable but coins are countable, and time is uncountable but minutes are countable. English is not describing the world here — it is describing the noun. Choose by the word on the page.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
